title: Nitzavim: those not here today (Deuteronomy 29:13–14)
hookLine: the covenant includes "him that is not here with us this day"

lines: AN OAK FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S SHADE.
cards: People do strange, hopeful things for strangers in the future. They bury time capsules with letters to readers not yet born. They write wills.
They plant oak trees that won't give real shade for decades. A town council approves a bridge that will outlast every person in the room.
Moses, standing before the whole camp on the plains of Moab, does something stranger than any of these. He makes a covenant binding on people who aren't there.

teach.b: "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath; but with him that standeth here with us this day before the LORD our God, and also with him that is not here with us this day." Who isn't there?
The plain reading: future generations. Children not yet born, and their children after them.
The Talmud, in Shevuot, reads it to include the generations to come and those who would one day join the Jewish people as converts.

The midrash goes further: the souls of all those generations were somehow present at that moment, standing in the covenant. That's why a convert is sometimes described as a soul that was already there, coming home.
Read it as mysticism or as poetry; either way the idea is plain. A covenant isn't only a contract between people in the same room. It reaches forward.
The people standing that day are holding something on behalf of people they'll never meet.

teach.h: THE ONES NOT HERE, NOW ARRIVED.
teach.b: Every generation since has been, in a sense, the ones who were not here, now arrived. This week ran through Ki Tavo and into Nitzavim. The first goes to thanks.
A wandering father. This day, new. Blessed coming and going.
Understanding takes years. All of you.
And today, those not yet here. A week that began with the farmer remembering his past, and ends with people far in the future.

how: Jewish teachers often cite this verse to explain why each generation counts itself part of the covenant, and why converts to Judaism are traditionally described as having been present when it was made.

games.q: you're making a promise whose results you'll never see. who does Moses say this covenant includes?
o: only the people in front of him.
those standing here today, and those not here.
games.why: both: those standing there that day, and those not yet born.

practice: Picture someone who'll be alive a hundred years from now: maybe a great-grandchild, maybe a stranger who'll walk your street and read the books you read.
What would you want to hand them: a habit, a story, a cleaner river, a kinder way of arguing? Let one small thing you're doing now be something they might someday stand on.
